opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first impression was that it was much more complicated than I expected. Coming from academia, and having written Tianshou, I was used to RL codebases where you can read the whole PPO implementation in an afternoon: a rollout loop, an advantage calculation, the clipped objective, and you're done.

At OpenAI the core algorithm was still recognizably PPO, but everything around it was a different world. The system was distributed across a lot of machines. Rollout workers, the training side, and evaluation all had to stay in sync. Many of the problems you hit weren't really RL problems in the textbook sense. They were engineering problems: throughput, stale data, numerical stability at scale, and making sure a small change didn't silently break something three components away.

What surprised me most was how much accumulated knowledge lived in the code. There were small details, like how things were normalized, how certain hyperparameters were scheduled, and little fixes people had added after running into instabilities. Each one looked minor, but together they made the difference between a run that works and one that falls apart. Some of that wasn't written down anywhere, so you learned it by reading code and asking people.

So my feeling was half "wow, this is impressive infrastructure" and half "there's a lot of room to make this cleaner and faster." That second part is a lot of what I ended up working on. I wanted to make the pipeline simpler to reason about and quicker to iterate on, because in RL, especially at that scale, iteration speed is really everything. If an experiment takes days and you can't trust the infrastructure, you just can't make progress on the research itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses OpenAI’s PPO pipeline, but does not identify GPT-3.5 supervised fine-tuning as the most widely used training approach when Jiayi Weng joined.

fable-5.1.text:
When I first joined, my background was mostly open-source RL — I'd built Tianshou, which is a small, clean PPO implementation, so I thought I understood PPO pretty well. Then I opened the internal codebase and honestly my first reaction was, "Wait, is this really PPO?"

On paper it's the same algorithm — clipped objective, GAE, value function. But the actual pipeline was dramatically more complicated than anything in a textbook or a research repo. The core algorithm was maybe a few hundred lines, and then there were thousands and thousands of lines around it: the distributed rollout system, how the samplers talked to the trainers, how the reward model got called, how KL to the reference policy was computed and controlled, all the mixed precision and sharding details. The "PPO" part was almost the smallest piece.

The second thing that struck me was how many small implementation details actually mattered. Things like advantage normalization, how you handle the value loss, how you tokenize and mask out the prompt, learning rate schedules — in academic RL these feel like footnotes, but at that scale, if you got one of them wrong, training would just quietly go sideways. It took a few days before I'd see that a run had drifted and you'd have to dig back through everything.

And the third thing was that a lot of the knowledge was tribal. There were people who knew why a particular flag was set to a particular value because of a failure from a year earlier, but it wasn't written down anywhere. So part of my early time was just reading code and asking a lot of "why is this here?" questions. Some of the answers were "it matters a lot," and some were "nobody remembers, don't touch it."

That experience is actually a big part of why I later cared so much about reproducing and documenting RLHF implementation details publicly — because I felt the gap between the simple textbook PPO and the real thing was way bigger than most people outside realized.

astra-6.text: I’d separate understanding PPO from understanding the whole training pipeline. The algorithm gives you the basic idea, but then you have to understand how rollout collection, reward computation, and policy updates fit together. That’s where I’d start: tracing one batch through the system and making sure I understood what each stage was doing.
